title: Prompt Interference in LLM Post-Training: Why Pass@k Optimization Can Degrade Pass@1
claim: Optimizing a multi-sample objective upweights hard, conflicting items, rotating the update away from the single-sample objective and hurting it.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: bar chart then two vector diagrams, red overlay
description: Three panels. (a) is a grouped bar chart of success rate for pass@1 and pass@k, with blue bars before and orange bars after pass@k optimization. Small arrows show pass@1 dropping from about 0.46 to 0.40 and pass@k rising from about 0.62 to 0.73. (b) is titled ∇pass@1. Gray arrows for prompts 1, 2 and 3 fan out from a common origin. Prompt 3 points up-left, against the other two. A thick black arrow, labeled average, points up-right. (c) is titled ∇pass@k in red. The same gray prompt arrows are overlaid with red dashed arrows, and the prompt 3 arrow is longer. A thick red average arrow now points up-left. A red arc marks the obtuse angle between it and the black pass@1 average. The eye goes first to the bar chart, then to the red arrow in (c).
caption: (a) Empirical trade-off. Under pass@$k$ policy optimization, pass@$k$ increases while pass@$1$ may decrease. We explain this empirically observed trade-off in (b) and (c), which schematically illustrate the pass@$1$ and pass@$k$ ($k>1$) gradients for three prompts and their expectations in policy-parameter space. (b) Pass@1 gradients with negatively interfering prompt. This panel shows a setting in which prompt $3$ is negatively interfering with prompts $1$ and $2$, i.e., the per-prompt pass@1 gradient for prompt $3$ has negative inner product with the per-prompt pass@$1$ gradients for prompts $1$ and $2$ (see Section [ref]). Here, $\nabla$pass@$1$ denotes the population pass@$1$ gradient, given by the average (expectation over prompts; here under a uniform distribution) of the per-prompt pass@$1$ gradients. (c) Pass@$k$ vs pass@1 gradient conflict. Per-prompt pass@k gradients are scaled versions of the corresponding per-prompt pass@1 gradients (Eq. [ref]). This reweighting amplifies the magnitude of the pass@$k$ gradient for the negatively interfering prompt $3$, causing the resulting population pass@$k$ gradient to conflict with the population pass@$1$ gradient (their inner product becomes negative, corresponding to an obtuse angle, shown here as approximately $120^\circ$). Hence, a policy update in the pass@$k$ gradient direction can increase pass@$k$ while decreasing pass@1.
abstract: Pass@$k$ is a widely used performance metric for verifiable large language model tasks, including mathematical reasoning, code generation, and short-answer reasoning. It defines success if any of $k$ independently sampled solutions passes a verifier. This multi-sample inference metric has motivated inference-aware fine-tuning methods that directly optimize pass@$k$. However, prior work reports a trade-off: pass@$k$ improves while pass@1 degrades under such methods. This trade-off is practically important because pass@1 often remains a hard operational constraint due to latency and cost budgets, imperfect verifier coverage, and the need for a reliable single-shot fallback. We study the origin of this trade-off and provide a theoretical characterization of when pass@$k$ policy optimization can reduce pass@1 through gradient conflict induced by prompt interference. This interference arises because shared model parameters couple prompts, so improving performance on some prompts can adversely affect others. We show that pass@$k$ policy gradients can conflict with pass@1 gradients because pass@$k$ optimization implicitly reweights prompts toward low-success prompts; when these prompts are negatively interfering, their upweighting can rotate the pass@$k$ update direction away from the pass@1 direction. We illustrate our findings with large language model experiments on verifiable mathematical reasoning and coding tasks.
